This appendix documents the 3D version of the room CFD model in

. The physics, the turbulence models, the advection schemes and the comfort indices are the same, and are only summarised here. The 3D model adds the room width: the side walls are real walls, and an opening can be narrower than the room, for example a window 1.2 m wide in a 4 m wide office. The model is made for comparing cases and seeing the physics. It does not give design values.
The model exists in three versions that give the same results:

children.value: The 3D room CFD app with a window 1.2 m wide, 0.9–2.1 m high, 16 °C supply air and 6 air changes per hour, on the coarse mesh a few seconds into a run. The heat source stands in the middle of the room.

A run simulates 30 minutes and averages the last 10. Before a run the section and the plan show the empty room with the window, the exhaust and the heat source. During a run they show the instantaneous field while the simulation runs and the time-averaged field when it finishes. Three sliders move the long section across the width, the plan up through the room and the cross section (parallel to the facade) back through the room; a dashed line in each view shows where the other two cut, and two checkboxes hide these lines and the occupied zone. The slider beside the colour bar draws one isoline on all three views, for example the 0.15 m/s air speed or the 20 % draught rate; each of the three views keeps its own value. The draught panel shows the key results with three charts of the air speed and the ISO 7730 draught rate: along x at ankle height in the long section, along y at ankle height in the cross section (both also with the ASHRAE 55 ankle draught), and from floor to ceiling where the two sections cross. The occupied zone (by default 0.6 m from all walls and 1.8 m high) can be resized, and a button draws the mesh on the three views. A convergence chart at the bottom, next to the exhaust temperature and the energy imbalance, shows the rates of change of velocity and temperature and the floor speed 1 m from the facade at the centre of the window.
The app is a single HTML file,
, with the solver inlined. Save it anywhere and double-click it to use it offline.

The room is by default 5 m deep (x), 4 m wide (y) and 2.5 m high (z), with the facade at x = 0. In the app the depth, width and height can be changed; the mesh is then set by the cell size (20, 10 or 5 cm), and the exhaust stays 0.1–0.2 m below the ceiling. The supply opening sits in the facade or the back wall and can have any width; it is centred unless

are given. The app offers the same opening types as the 2D app (a window, a balcony door, a top hatch and a low slot, plus a window across the full width), and the opening can be slid along the facade. The exhaust is in the back wall or the ceiling. The heat gains are a box standing on the floor. In the app it is by default 0.6 m deep, 0.8 m wide and 1.2 m high in the middle of the room, and it can be moved and resized, or placed by clicking in the plan; the Python examples use a box 0.4 m deep and 1.2 m high across the full width at x = 2.3–2.7 m. With a height of 0 it becomes a heated patch of floor (
), which heats the air through the floor surface, as a sun patch does. The power is sized as in the 2D model so that the well-mixed room temperature is the same in every case:

Furniture is solid and adiabatic. A box takes the cells whose centres lie inside it: the faces of those cells are closed, so no air or heat passes, and the cells stay at the start temperature (grey in the app). A box must therefore be at least one cell thick. Furniture with zero size along one axis is a thin plate, such as a table top or a partition. It sits on the grid plane nearest to it and closes the cell faces in that plane, so it blocks the flow without taking up cells. On both sides of a plate, and on the faces of a box, the velocity parallel to the surface has no slip, with the log-law wall shear when k-ε is used.

children.value: on the cell faces, the projection method with an explicit time step, and TVD (van Leer) or upwind advection. The default grid is 50 × 40 × 25 cells (10 cm), which is 50,000 cells against 5,000 in the 2D section.

The pressure equation is the costly part in 3D. A direct solver, as used in 2D, does not scale: on 50,000 cells the LU factor has about 27 million entries. The 3D model therefore solves the pressure equation iteratively, with conjugate gradients preconditioned by one multigrid V-cycle

. The cells are grouped 2 × 2 × 2 into coarser grids until fewer than a few hundred cells are left, the error is smoothed by weighted Jacobi sweeps on each grid, and the coarsest grid is solved directly. Each time step starts from the pressure of the previous step and stops when the residual has fallen by a factor
, which changes the temperatures by less than
. The number of iterations hardly grows with the number of cells, typically 3–10 per time step.

turns each stage of the time step into one compiled loop over the cells, run in parallel on all processor cores. The pressure solve still takes about 80 % of the run time, so the gain is a factor of about 2 (see the run times below).

runs the whole time loop on the graphics card, including the time step and the dot products of the pressure solver, so data only comes back to the page for plotting. The differences from the Python version are:
Single precision, because WGSL has no double precision. Temperature is stored as the deviation from the start value to keep the small changes per time step.

The multigrid uses plain aggregation with 7-point coarse operators (half the Galerkin product), so every grid level is a simple stencil that runs well on a GPU, and an exact solve on the coarsest grid of at most 128 cells.
